prediction:
1. Scleritis (including posterior scleritis) — deep, boring unilateral orbital pain in a 59-year-old with gradual onset is most consistent; often severe, may not have obvious external swelling early.
2. Primary headache disorder with orbital pain (migraine, ocular migraine) — unilateral orbital/retro-orbital pain can present over days, may be intermittent and without clear local eye findings.
3. Cluster headache (episodic trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia) — can cause severe unilateral periorbital pain in bouts over days; consider if pain is severe and associated with lacrimation/nasal symptoms.
4. Giant cell (temporal) arteritis — age >50 with new orbital/head pain places this on the differential because of risk of vision loss; may present without obvious systemic symptoms early.
5. Optic neuritis — painful eye movement and potential visual changes can present as unilateral orbital pain; less likely at this age but remains possible.

Clinical next steps I would have requested earlier (urgent when any vision change or systemic symptoms): focused ocular exam (visual acuity, pupils with relative afferent pupillary defect check, extraocular movements, intraocular pressure, slit-lamp exam for scleral injection/uveitis, fundoscopic exam), ESR and CRP (for giant cell arteritis), and urgent orbital/brain MRI with contrast and/or CT orbits if concern for posterior scleritis, optic neuritis, or orbital cellulitis; refer urgently to ophthalmology if any vision loss, marked redness/swelling, or elevated suspicion for GCA.
